items.title: The set of elements for which the obstruction to derived completeness vanishes is a radical ideal
items.author: The Stacks Project Authors
items.work: Stacks Project, chapter more-algebra.tex (More on Algebra)

items.difficulty_reason: The lemma takes a ring A and an object K of D(A) and asserts that the set I of elements f in A with T(K, f) = 0 is a radical ideal of A (source lines 25935-25939). The proof uses the characterisation of the condition T(K, f) = 0 in terms of the vanishing of Ext^n_A(A_f, K) for all n, which is the content of the preceding lemma and is invoked without further mention (proof lines 25942-25943). The three ideal axioms are then checked. Closure under multiplication is immediate: if f lies in I and g is arbitrary, then A_{gf} is an A_f-module, so Ext^n_A(A_{gf}, K) = 0 for all n and hence gf lies in I (proof lines 25944-25945). Additivity is the substantive step: for f and g in I the proof exhibits the short exact sequence 0 -> A_{f+g} -> A_{f(f+g)} oplus A_{g(f+g)} -> A_{gf(f+g)} -> 0, which holds because f and g generate the unit ideal in A_{f+g}, using the standard covering lemma and the surjectivity of the last arrow (proof lines 25946-25952). Applying the long exact sequence of Ext and the vanishing of the three Ext groups appearing in the outer positions for all n then gives the vanishing of Ext^n_A(A_{f+g}, K) for all n, so f + g lies in I (proof lines 25952-25957). Finally the radical property is immediate because T(K, f) = T(K, f^n), or equivalently because A_f is isomorphic to A_{f^n}, so f^n in I implies f in I (proof lines 25958-25959). The non-routine content is the standard covering short exact sequence that makes additivity work.
